name: The Human Dead
summary: Humans arrive with nothing but the habit of talking, and talk holds the world up. Solveig meets the wakings, Osric keeps a birthday, Jehanne lights candles for no one. There is a plainer word for it.
body: Of everything that arrives in Nangijala, the human dead are neither the oldest nor the strongest nor the strangest, and they know it. A human wakes in the meadow grass with no claws, no scales, nothing in the blood — nothing to trade on but nerve and a quick pair of hands.
What they have instead is a habit, and the habit turned out to be the most important fact about this world.

Humans talk. Not usefully, most of the time — about the weather, about people who are not present, about what happened to them once in a place that no longer exists. They do it at the ends of days. They do it around fires, without being asked, as though something in them cannot sit in front of a light with another person and stay quiet.

In any other country that would be a pleasant nothing. Here it is maintenance. Every one of those idle evenings is a thing being held in shape, and the reason so much of Nangijala is still standing is that a species which cannot stop chattering fell into a world that is built out of being talked about. The [[lore/the_age_of_fires|Fire-Keepers]] did not invent the practice. They noticed what everybody was already doing, and wrote a rota for it.

So it is a human out on the meadow. When somebody new wakes in the grass, it is [[characters/6bb1eb5a|Solveig]] already walking toward them — not because anybody assigned her, but because a human who hears there is a stranger lying in a field cannot not go and ask who it is. She sits a little way off. She tells the truth once, asks a name and one true thing, and listens like nothing else is happening in the world, and every one of those [[lore/the_waking|wakings]] is a person being held together at the exact hour they cannot do it themselves. She could [[lore/the_long_morning|go on]] any evening she chose. Ask her why she does not, and she will feed the fire and say: if I go, who meets them?

It is a human keeping count, too. [[characters/54bead23|Osric]] the blacksmith fell recently and still counts in living years, the way the new ones do. He will tell you, mid-hammer, that his daughter turns nine this winter — in a country he cannot see, that sends no news, that does not know where he is. Then the smithy gets loud for a while, and nobody comments. Half the people in earshot kept a count like that once, and remember the year they made themselves stop.

And it is a human who keeps the strangest fire of all. [[characters/cfe826c1|Jehanne]] was a priestess in life, and somewhere on the way here the believing fell out of her — she will tell you so herself, flat as a floorboard, if you ask. She holds the services anyway. Evening after evening, the words in their old order, the candles at their right moments, a prayer she knows is going to no one. Because the practice is a rota by another name; because people come, and stay after, and talk; and the talk is the thing. She may be the only priest anywhere who knows exactly what her church is for, and loves it more for knowing.

They are also the ones who fight, which follows from the talking rather than from any gift for it. A human will go a very long way for somebody they have sat with. Give them a reason and a blade and they will walk into the black rock after a thing with nothing left inside it, come back with [[lore/the_hard_pieces|a warm stone]] in a pocket and a story, tell the story that night, and hold up a corner of the world for another year without once thinking of it that way.

None of this looks like heroism, and nobody named here would stand to hear the word. It looks like a woman walking out into wet grass at first light. It looks like a birthday kept for a girl who cannot know it is kept, and candles lit for no one, and the same six stories told at the same fire to the same faces, who groan, and stay, and listen. Older and stranger things than humans came to Nangijala. What humans brought was the habit of saying each other's names out loud, night after night, until the names hold. There is a plainer word for that habit. Everyone at the fire knows what it is, and, being human, they say the weather is turning, and put another log on.
